subtitle: Turn awareness into change by choosing one process, testing a change through plan, try, study and adjust, sharing decisions with the people affected, and measuring results in the work rather than by tracking people.
audience: For DHS and DSD leaders, supervisors, program and policy staff, equity committee members, and teams ready to act on what they learned in this pathway.

lessons.title: From awareness to one process
objectives: Explain why a team moves from awareness to action by choosing one process rather than many goals.
Select a specific process the team owns or can influence, and describe it from the side of the person who receives it.
Map what binds the process and who has authority to change it.
Connect the choice to the DHS Equity Policy expectation to use an equity lens and the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit.
lessons.teaching:
This pathway began with awareness: noticing culture, seeing how it shapes systems, and using lenses such as Okun's framework to make familiar norms visible. Awareness is necessary, and it is not the same as change. A team that has finished a learning series often has more insight than it can use and a long list of things it would like to be different. Lists of that kind tend to stall, because no single item has an owner, a scope or a date. The step from awareness to action usually begins with narrowing: choosing one process, describing it concretely, agreeing to change something about it, and learning from the result.

A good first process has four features. It is specific and observable, such as a notice people receive, an intake step, the way a meeting with community partners is run, or the way interview questions are set. It affects people in ways the team can learn about, including people with disabilities, families and partners who are rarely asked. It sits within the team's authority or close to it. And it is small enough to change and study within a few months. "Improve our culture" is not a process. "Revise the letter people receive when a service plan change is denied, and test whether people understand what they can do next" is one. The lenses from earlier modules can help with the choice. Perfectionism or worship of the written word might point to the letter, and power hoarding might point to how decisions about an intake step get made.

Before changing anything, map what binds the process. Some features are set by federal or state law or rule, some by DHS or division policy, some by contract, and some by habit. Find out who owns each piece and who can approve a change. The map prevents two common failures: a team spending months on a feature it cannot change, and a team changing a feature that was required. Where a requirement comes from law, the team may still be able to reduce its burden through a clearer explanation, more time where the rule permits it, or alternative formats. Legal questions go to legal counsel, and formal civil-rights or accommodation questions go to the responsible office.

The DHS Equity Policy (version 2.0, effective August 2023) asks staff to apply an equity lens in daily work and to use the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit, which is posted on the agency's internal equity page, in agency work, planning meetings and actions that need leadership approval. It calls for a formal analysis of actions with prolonged or long-term impact that need approval from a supervisor or a more senior leader, and it asks each administration or area to work with its Equity Director and Equity Committee on goals with measurable outcomes. Choosing one process gives that policy something concrete to work on. It also lets the team begin with the opening questions of the State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit: what is the proposed change, what outcomes do we want, and which groups are likely to be affected positively or negatively?
lessons.keyPoint: Action starts by narrowing: one concrete process, a map of what binds it and who decides, and a clear statement of the change and the outcome you want.
lessons.example: Practice case: After the team completes this pathway, {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} collects 14 ideas on a whiteboard, from "slow down" to "rewrite all our letters" to "more community voice." Everyone agrees with nearly all of them. {{SUPERVISOR}} asks what the team will actually do next quarter, and the room goes quiet.
lessons.question: What should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} propose?
choices: Pick one process from the list, such as the denial letter for service plan changes, map who owns it and what binds it, and define one change to test with people who receive the letter.
Assign each idea to a different team member so that all 14 move forward at once.
Set the list aside until the team has completed more training, so that any changes are well informed.
feedback: This turns broad agreement into work the team can do, own and learn from. The other ideas stay on the list for later cycles.
Spreading 14 efforts across individuals leaves each one small, isolated and hard to study, and it puts the load on whoever has the least time to say no.
More learning can help, but the team already has enough insight to test one change. Waiting for complete knowledge is how awareness stays awareness.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider which process in your own work you would choose first, or use the practice case. What makes it a good candidate, and what makes you hesitate?
lessons.action: Write a one-paragraph description of one process your team owns: what it is, who it affects, what a person on the receiving end experiences, and what binds it (law, rule, policy, contract or habit). Name who can approve a change, and bring the description to your supervisor or team.

check.question: Which is the best example of a process to start with?
check.correct: The letter people receive when a service plan change is denied.
wrong: Making the division's culture more inclusive.
Changing how every program in DHS engages communities.
check.feedback: A good starting process is specific, observable, within or near the team's authority, and small enough to change and study. Broad goals matter, but they are reached through concrete processes.

lessons.title: Plan, try, study, adjust: measure the work, not people
objectives: Describe a plan, try, study and adjust cycle, including a written prediction and a small test.
Choose measures that show change in the work, such as clearer notices, barriers removed or community input that led to a documented change.
Explain why progress is never measured by tracking individual staff, learners or community members.
Decide after a test whether to adapt, adopt or abandon a change.
lessons.teaching:
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services publishes a plan, do, study, act template for quality improvement, and this pathway uses the same cycle in plainer words: plan, try, study, adjust. In planning, the team names the change it will test, predicts what will happen and why, and designs a small test: who is involved (ideally the staff who do the work), how long it will run, what it needs, and what information will be collected. In the try step, the team runs the test on a small scale and writes down what actually happens, including problems and surprises. In the study step, the team compares the results with the prediction and looks for unintended consequences. In the adjust step, the team decides whether to adapt the change and test again, adopt it more widely, or abandon it and try another approach. The template expects most improvement to take more than one cycle.

The prediction matters more than it seems, because writing "we expect fewer calls asking what the letter means, and more people requesting a review before the deadline" turns a good intention into something the team can check. It also guards against a common trap, which is declaring success because a change was made. A revised notice is an output; whether people understand it and can act on it is the outcome, and only the outcome tells you whether a barrier came down.

Measure change in the work, not in people: useful measures describe what a process does for the people who use it: a notice that people who receive it find clearer, fewer missed deadlines, a barrier removed (a phone-only step that now has a written option), shorter waits, or community input that led to a documented change, with a record of what was suggested, what was decided and why. Some measures are counts and some are short descriptions, and both are evidence. What the cycle never does is track people, which means it does not score individual staff on their attitudes, treat course completion as a sign of progress, monitor how colleagues speak in meetings, or collect information about community members beyond what the program already needs and is authorized to keep. Reflections in this pathway stay private. When results are broken out by group, check definitions and small counts, and use approved privacy protections so that no one can be identified.

The State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit asks how a policy or program's impact will be monitored over time, what metrics will be used to evaluate success and identify areas for improvement, and what mechanisms are in place to ensure accountability. A plan, try, study and adjust cycle answers those questions in a practical way. Keep the measures few, decide in advance when you will look, and include people affected in the study step where you can, because they can often explain a result that the numbers cannot. Then record the decision and the reason for it. An adjusted plan is not a failure; it is the cycle doing what it was designed to do.
lessons.keyPoint: Predict, test small, compare and decide. Measure what the process does for people, such as clearer notices, barriers removed and documented changes from community input, and never measure progress by tracking individuals.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{SUPERVISOR}}'s team has revised the denial letter and wants to show leadership that the work is succeeding. One proposal is to report how many staff completed equity training and to survey staff about their personal bias before and after. {{CASE_MANAGER}} suggests looking instead at calls about the letter and at review requests over the next two months.
lessons.question: Which measurement plan fits this course's approach?
choices: Report training completion and the staff bias survey, since leadership expects numbers.
Track which case managers send the letters that lead to the most complaints, so that coaching can be targeted.
Predict what the new letter will change, then track calls asking what it means, on-time review requests and feedback from a few people who received it, and report what the team learned.
feedback: Completion counts and self-reported attitudes describe training activity, not the letter. They can also make staff feel monitored, which weakens the safety this work depends on.
This turns a process study into individual monitoring. Letter outcomes usually reflect the template and the rules more than the person sending it, and performance concerns have their own channels.
This measures what the letter does for the people who receive it, sets a prediction to compare against, and includes their account. It tells leadership whether the change helped.
lessons.reflection: Privately think about how progress on equity or culture is reported in your area, or use the practice case. Does the report describe changes in the work or activity by people, and what would a work-based measure look like?
lessons.action: For the process you chose in lesson 1, write a one-page plan: the change, your prediction and why, a small test with dates and the people involved, two or three measures of the work (not of people), and the date you will study the results.

check.question: Which is a measure of change in the work?
check.correct: The number of people who requested a review on time after a notice was revised.
wrong: The percentage of staff who completed an equity course.
Individual staff scores on a survey about personal bias.
check.feedback: Measures of the work describe what a process does for the people who use it. Completion rates and attitude scores describe people and activity, and they do not show whether a barrier was removed.

lessons.title: Power hoarding, paternalism and participatory decisions
objectives: Describe how power hoarding and paternalism can show up in well-intended public service decisions.
Distinguish levels of engagement, from informing and consulting to collaboration and shared decision-making.
State in advance what is open to input, what is fixed, and who decides.
Report decisions and their reasons back to the people who took part.
lessons.teaching:
Okun's framework names power hoarding and paternalism among its characteristics, and they belong in a module about action because they often grow from good intentions. Power hoarding can look like a leader making every substantive decision before others can respond, keeping decision criteria private, or treating a request to share decisions as a challenge to authority. Paternalism can look like deciding what people need without them, explaining choices only to those who already hold authority, or treating people who use services as recipients of help rather than as people with expertise about their own lives. Disability rights advocates have pressed this point for decades under the call "nothing about us without us." A manager who protects a schedule, or a team that wants to spare families another meeting, may sincerely believe it is serving people well. The question is not motive but who shaped the decision and who has to live with it.

Participatory decision-making does not mean everyone decides everything. It means being clear about the level of participation on offer and then honoring it. The State of Minnesota describes engagement in its Equity Analysis Toolkit as a range that includes informing, consulting, involvement, collaboration and empowering people. Each level has a place: informing fits when a decision is already fixed by law, and consulting asks for reactions to a draft. Collaboration means working with partners on the problem and the options. Empowering places a decision with the people most affected, within what the agency can authorize. Trouble starts when a team calls something collaboration after it has already decided, or invites input on questions that are not actually open. People notice, and the next invitation is harder for them to accept.

Several practices keep participation honest, and the first comes before engagement starts: write down what is open, what is fixed and why, who makes the final decision, and when. Involve people early, while options are still real, rather than asking them to react to a finished product. Make participation accessible through plain language, alternative formats, interpreters, accommodations, and times that work for people with jobs and caregiving responsibilities. Work with Tribal Nations through the applicable government-to-government process rather than treating consultation as an ordinary stakeholder meeting. Inside a team, the same logic applies to staff: share the criteria for a decision, ask the people who do the work, and explain the final call. The DHS Equity Policy calls for authentic, meaningful and ongoing community engagement, and it describes engagement as co-creating solutions with people who understand barriers from their own experience.

The last step is the report back, and the State toolkit asks how partners will be kept informed and involved during implementation, and it suggests sharing the analysis with groups that are disproportionately affected and making the documents accessible. Say what was decided, how input shaped it, what was not adopted and why, and what happens next. That record is also one of the measures from the previous lesson: community input that led to a documented change. Over time, a team can look back across its decisions and ask an honest question about its own pattern. How often did input change the result, and whose input was it?
lessons.keyPoint: State the level of participation before you start, involve people while options are still open, make participation accessible, and report back what was decided and how input shaped it.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} is redesigning how people request a change to their service plan. The plan is to finish the new process internally and then present it to a self-advocate advisory group for feedback two weeks before launch. {{COMMUNITY_PARTNER}}, who supports the advisory group, says members have said they are tired of being asked to react to decisions that are already made.
lessons.question: What should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} do?
choices: Keep the plan, but make the presentation more interactive so members feel heard.
Meet with the advisory group now, explain which parts of the process are fixed by rule and which are open, work through the open options together, and agree on how decisions will be reported back.
Leave the advisory group out this time to avoid adding to their frustration, and rely on staff expertise.
feedback: A better presentation does not change the level of participation. Members would still be reacting to a finished product, which is exactly what they said they are tired of.
This moves engagement earlier, is honest about limits, shares real choices with the people most affected, and builds in accountability for what happens with their input.
Leaving people out because past engagement went poorly repeats the paternalism the partner described. The remedy is better participation, not less.
lessons.reflection: Privately think about a decision in your work that affected people who were not part of shaping it, or use the practice case. What level of participation was actually offered, and what level would have fit?
lessons.action: For the process you chose in lesson 1, write a short participation plan: what is fixed and why, what is open, who decides and by when, the level of engagement you will offer each group affected, how you will make it accessible, and how you will report back.

check.question: What is the main problem when a team invites collaboration on a decision it has already made?
check.correct: The participation actually offered does not match what was promised, which erodes trust in later engagement.
wrong: Collaboration is never appropriate for a public agency.
Partners should only be informed, never consulted.
check.feedback: Each level of engagement has a place. The problem is a mismatch between what a team says it is offering and what it actually offers. Being clear about what is open, and honoring it, keeps engagement credible.

lessons.title: Sustaining the work and the limits of training alone
objectives: Summarize what research on diversity training suggests about its effects on attitudes and behavior.
Explain why training is a support for change rather than evidence of it.
Build sustaining features into a change: an owner, a place in standard work, a review date and a report back.
Plan for the well-being of the people who carry the work.
lessons.teaching:
Training can build shared language, and this pathway hopes it has. It is still fair to ask what training alone can do. A meta-analysis by Bezrukova, Spell, Perry and Jehn, published in Psychological Bulletin in 2016, combined 260 samples from more than 40 years of research on diversity training. It found that effects on reactions and on attitudes tended to decay over time, that effects on what people learned held up better, and that effects were greater when training was complemented by other diversity initiatives. A preregistered field experiment by Chang and colleagues, published in 2019 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, tested a one-hour online diversity training with about 3,000 employees of a large global company. The training shifted some attitudes, but its effects on workplace behavior were mostly absent or limited to some groups, and the authors concluded that one-off trainings "are unlikely to be stand-alone solutions."

These studies have limits. They cover many kinds of training in many settings, and neither one studied DSD or a learning pathway like this one. Still, their direction is consistent, and it matches what many people see at work: knowing more does not by itself change how a process works. That is why this pathway never treats completion as change, and why the measures in lesson 2 look at the work. Training is best understood as one support among several. It can help a team notice a pattern, share a vocabulary, and feel more able to raise a concern. The change itself happens in notices, steps, decisions and routines, and it lasts only if those are built to last.

Sustaining the work means giving it a structure that survives busy seasons and staff turnover. Each change needs an owner, a place in standard work (a procedure, template, checklist or recurring agenda item rather than one person's memory), a date to look again, and a report back to the people affected. The DHS Equity Policy offers a structure to connect with: each administration or area works with its Equity Director and Equity Committee on goals with measurable outcomes, and the equity analysis asks how an initiative will be sustained through funding and implementation strategies. A team can link its cycle to that structure instead of running it alone. Keep a short record of each cycle, covering what was tried, what was learned and what was decided, so that the next person does not have to start from zero.

Sustaining the work also means sustaining the people doing it. Equity and culture work often falls to a few colleagues, frequently those with lived experience of the barriers under discussion, and usually on top of a full workload. That pattern reproduces the urgency and individualism this pathway asks teams to examine. Share the load, recognize the work when assignments are made, pace cycles realistically, and accept that some cycles will show that a change did not help. That finding is useful rather than embarrassing. The goal is not to prove that the team is good; it is to keep making the work fairer for the people it serves, one process at a time, and to keep going after the first cycle ends.
lessons.keyPoint: Research suggests one-off training rarely changes behavior on its own. Treat training as a support, put each change into standard work with an owner and a review date, and share the load so the work lasts.
lessons.example: Practice case: The division's equity committee is setting next year's goals. One proposal makes 100 percent completion of this pathway by all staff the main goal. {{SUPERVISOR}}, a committee member, has watched two teams finish the pathway and return to old routines within a few months. {{NEW_COLLEAGUE}}, also on the committee, asks what the goal would look like if it were about the work instead.
lessons.question: What should {{SUPERVISOR}} suggest?
choices: Keep completion as one supporting goal and add goals about the work: each team runs at least one plan, try, study and adjust cycle on a process, with an owner, a review date and a report back to the people affected.
Drop the pathway, since research shows that training does not work.
Make completion the only goal, since it is the easiest result to track and report.
feedback: This keeps training in a supporting role and makes the goal about changes people can see in the work, with the structure that helps those changes last.
The research shows limits, not uselessness. Effects were greater when training was paired with other efforts, and pairing is exactly what this option gives up.
Completion is easy to count, but it measures activity rather than change, and the research suggests it is unlikely to change behavior on its own.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider a change you have seen fade after its first burst of energy, or use the practice case. What would have helped it last: an owner, a routine, a review date, a report back, or a more widely shared load?
lessons.action: For the process you chose in this course, write a sustaining plan: who owns the change, where it will live in standard work, when you will review it, how you will report back to the people affected, and how the work will be shared. Bring the plan to your supervisor or your area's Equity Committee.

check.question: What does the 2016 meta-analysis by Bezrukova and colleagues suggest about diversity training?
check.correct: Effects on attitudes tended to fade over time, and effects were greater when training was paired with other initiatives.
wrong: A single session reliably changes workplace behavior.
Training has no measurable effects of any kind.
check.feedback: The meta-analysis found effects that differed by outcome, with attitude effects decaying and learning holding up better. Effects were greater when training was complemented by other diversity efforts, which supports pairing learning with changes in the work.

cards.back: A specific, observable process within or near the team's authority, small enough to change and study in a few months.
Predict and plan a small test, run it, compare the results with the prediction, then adapt, adopt or abandon the change.
A revised notice is an output. Whether people understand it and can act on it is the outcome.
Clearer notices, barriers removed, community input that led to a documented change. Never staff attitude scores, completion as progress, or tracking individuals.
Decisions and criteria stay with a few people. The alternative is participatory decision-making with a clearly stated level of engagement.
Deciding what people need without them. The alternative is involving people early, while options are still open.
Research suggests one-off training rarely changes behavior by itself, and effects are greater when training is paired with other efforts.

aid.heading: Choose one process
items: Name the process concretely and describe it from the side of the person who receives it.
Map what binds it: law, rule, policy, contract or habit.
Identify who can approve a change, and route legal or civil-rights questions to the responsible office.
Use the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit, as the DHS Equity Policy directs, especially for changes that need leadership approval or have long-term impact.

aid.heading: Run the cycle
items: Write a prediction and the reason for it.
Plan a small test with dates and the staff who do the work.
Study results against the prediction, including unintended consequences and the account of people affected.
Adapt, adopt or abandon, and record the decision and why.

aid.heading: Measure the work
items: Choose two or three measures of what the process does for people.
Count community input that led to a documented change, with what was suggested, decided and why.
Do not track individual staff, learners or community members, and do not treat completion as change.
Check definitions and small counts, and use approved privacy protections.

aid.heading: Share decisions and sustain the change
items: Before engagement, state what is open, what is fixed and who decides.
Report back what was decided, how input shaped it and what was not adopted.
Give each change an owner, a place in standard work and a review date.
Share the load, and connect the cycle with your Equity Director and Equity Committee.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services, Equity Policy
sources.note: Agency policy (version 2.0, effective August 4, 2023). Supports the expectations to apply an equity lens, use the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit, complete a formal analysis for long-term actions needing approval, set measurable goals with Equity Directors and Committees, and engage communities (lessons 1, 3 and 4). This course is learning material, not a substitute for the policy.

sources.title: State of Minnesota — Equity Analysis Toolkit: A Quick Guide
sources.note: Supports the impact assessment, monitoring and evaluation, accountability and partner-communication questions (lessons 1 to 3). A state-government tool; the DHS toolkit on the agency's internal site governs DHS analyses.

sources.title: State of Minnesota, Equity Analysis Toolkit
sources.note: Supports the description of engagement as a range from informing and consulting to involvement, collaboration and empowering (lesson 3).

sources.title: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services — PDSA Cycle Template (QAPI)
sources.note: Adapted from this federal template. Supports planning a small test with a prediction, involving staff who do the work, looking for unintended consequences, and adapt, adopt or abandon (lesson 2). Written for nursing homes.

sources.title: Bezrukova, Spell, Perry and Jehn — A Meta-Analytical Integration of Over 40 Years of Research on Diversity Training Evaluation, Psychological Bulletin 142(11), 2016 (Cornell eCommons copy)
sources.note: Supports the findings that attitude effects decayed, learning effects held up better, and effects were greater when training was complemented by other initiatives (lesson 4). Pools many kinds of training; it does not evaluate DSD or this pathway.

sources.title: Chang and colleagues — The Mixed Effects of Online Diversity Training, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 116(16), 2019
sources.note: A preregistered field experiment with about 3,000 employees of one global company. Supports the finding that a one-hour online training moved some attitudes but had mostly null behavioral effects (lesson 4). One organization and one training format.

sources.title: Tema Okun, White Supremacy Culture: Characteristics (updated 2025)
sources.note: The framework behind this pathway's leadership lens. The course uses power hoarding and paternalism as prompts for examining decisions, not as labels for people (lessons 1 and 3). Okun describes the list as drawn from practice and reflection rather than formal research.
